summary:
Bolivia's 2016 Gender Identity Law grants legal recognition on the basis of self-declared identity through an administrative procedure, permitting a change of name and gender marker without surgery or a medical diagnosis. Gender identity is a protected ground in the country's anti-discrimination legislation.

The 2009 Constitution prohibits discrimination and protects bodily integrity, with Article 15(II) addressing violence and Article 45(V) addressing maternity; Penal Code Title VIII governs abortion. The US State Department's 2011 Human Rights Report on Bolivia documented the constitutional guarantee against discrimination alongside persistent societal discrimination against LGBT people.

The 2016 statute was enacted despite low voter support for trans rights. Trans activists secured access to legislators of the ruling party, and heteronormative provisions were adopted in the same period because organised religion and LGBT organisations were both constituencies of the party in government. Contradictory laws therefore stand side by side.

Regional and international developments followed: an Inter-American Court of Human Rights opinion in January 2018, and in December 2020 civil-registry recognition of free union for same-sex couples.

Homosexuality remains taboo in Bolivia's armed forces. Reporting from August 2014 documented gay soldiers describing discrimination and sanctions, with testimony given anonymously; the TLGB collective and human-rights activists have demanded openness in the military.

Bolivia's first virtual survey of LGBTI people, published in December 2024, found what organisers described as the great exclusion of LGBTI people in the country.
tangentialFactors:
A July 2017 Newsweek count identified 18 countries believed to fully legalise LGBT military service following the US trans military ban; Bolivia was not singled out in that count, leaving its formal policy on trans service unresolved in these sources.

The US State Department's 2011 Human Rights Report on Bolivia also addresses arbitrary deprivation of life, prison conditions, and corruption as part of its general country assessment, which frames the broader human-rights environment in which anti-discrimination guarantees operate.
localsOnly:
Residents seeking to change legal name and gender marker do so through an administrative procedure under the 2016 law, without a requirement of surgery or medical diagnosis.

Constitutional protections against discrimination and bodily integrity, and the Penal Code provisions on abortion, form part of the domestic legal framework that residents can invoke.

Same-sex couples have had free union recognised by the civil registry since December 2020.

Service members face an environment described as hostile to openly LGBT personnel, with documented discrimination and sanctions reported as of 2014.
outOfScopeNotes:
Whether the 2016 Gender Identity Law's protections are enforced in practice, and how frequently name or marker changes are granted or refused, is not resolved in the available sources.

Bolivia's current formal policy on trans military service is unresolved; the 2017 Newsweek count did not address it specifically.

The specific content of the heteronormative provisions adopted alongside the 2016 law is not detailed in the inventory beyond the general characterisation.

The 2024 survey's methodology and sample are not described in the inventory, so the scale of exclusion it reports cannot be verified here.
